```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
```

## summarise() turns many rows into one

```{r}
#| label: toy
people <- tibble(
  WEIGHT = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
  TotInc = c(14, 13, 12, 8, 10),
  CMA    = c("x", "x", "y", "y", "y")
)

people |> summarise(avg_income = mean(TotInc), population = sum(WEIGHT))
```

## Weighted and unweighted averages differ

```{r}
#| label: weighted
people |>
  summarise(unweighted = mean(TotInc),
            weighted = weighted.mean(TotInc, w = WEIGHT))
```

Each row represents `WEIGHT` people, so the weighted average describes the population.

Other summary functions: `sum()`, `median()`, `min()`, `max()`, and `n()` (number of rows).

## group_by() makes summarise() work per group

```{r}
#| label: group
people |>
  group_by(CMA) |>
  summarise(population = sum(WEIGHT),
            avg_income = weighted.mean(TotInc, w = WEIGHT))
```

## Predict the output

```{r}
#| label: predict-code
#| eval: false
people |>
  filter(TotInc > 9) |>
  group_by(CMA) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: predict-out
#| echo: false
people |>
  filter(TotInc > 9) |>
  group_by(CMA) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

`n()` counts rows, not people. Use `sum(WEIGHT)` for people.
:::

## summarise() removes one level of grouping

```{r}
#| label: groups
two_levels <- people |>
  mutate(group = c("a", "b", "a", "b", "b")) |>
  group_by(CMA, group) |>
  summarise(population = sum(WEIGHT))
group_vars(two_levels)
```

The result is still grouped by `CMA`. Later steps then work within each CMA, which may not be what you want.

::: {.key-point}
Add `.groups = "drop"` to `summarise()`, or call `ungroup()`, when you are done with groups.
:::

## group_by() + mutate() keeps every row

```{r}
#| label: group-mutate
tb <- tibble(a = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2), b = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4))
tb |>
  group_by(a) |>
  mutate(share_of_group = b / sum(b)) |>
  ungroup()
```

## lag() looks at the previous row

```{r}
#| label: lag
tb |>
  group_by(a) |>
  mutate(previous = lag(b), change = b - lag(b)) |>
  ungroup()
```

## Application: average prices by year

```{r}
#| label: avg-price
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")

avg_price <- bca |>
  mutate(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year) |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

avg_price |> head(3)
```

## Check the last date before you compare years

```{r}
#| label: partial-year
bca |>
  filter(year(sale_date) >= 2024) |>
  group_by(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(sales = n(), first_sale = min(sale_date), last_sale = max(sale_date))
```

::: {.warning}
The file ends on `r paste(mday(max(bca$sale_date)), format(max(bca$sale_date), "%B %Y"))`. On a chart by year, 2026 looks like a collapse in sales, and its average covers only winter sales. Drop incomplete years, or compare the same months in each year.
:::

## An average can fall while every type rises

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: mix-shift
bca |>
  filter(year(sale_date) %in% 2016:2017) |>
  group_by(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(all = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
            sf = mean(price[act_use_cat == "S/F Res"], na.rm = TRUE),
            strata = mean(price[act_use_cat == "Strata Res"], na.rm = TRUE),
            sf_share = mean(act_use_cat == "S/F Res"))
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: mix-shift-numbers
#| include: false
mix <- bca |>
  filter(year(sale_date) %in% 2016:2017) |>
  group_by(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(sf_share = mean(act_use_cat == "S/F Res"))
```

::: {.key-point}
Both types rose in 2017, yet the average fell, because single-family homes dropped from `r round(100 * mix$sf_share[1])`% to `r round(100 * mix$sf_share[2])`% of sales. An average price describes the mix of homes sold. Compare within types, or use a regression (deck 17).
:::

## Practice: a price index

Using `avg_price`, compute a price index for each `act_use_cat`: the average price divided by the average price in **2010**.

## Answer

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: index
price_index <- avg_price |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  mutate(index_2010 = avg_price / avg_price[sale_year == 2010]) |>
  ungroup()

price_index |> filter(sale_year %in% c(2010, 2020))
```

## Row positions are fragile

An AI might write `nth(avg_price, 11)` for "the 2010 value", because 2010 is the 11th year:

```{r}
#| label: nth
avg_price |>
  arrange(desc(sale_year)) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(nth_11 = sale_year[11])
```

::: {.warning}
After a different sort, or with a missing year, the 11th row is no longer 2010. Select the year by its value, as in `avg_price[sale_year == 2010]`.
:::

## Practice: annual growth

Compute the annual growth rate of `avg_price` for each `act_use_cat`: (this year − last year) / last year.

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: growth
avg_price |>
  arrange(act_use_cat, sale_year) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  mutate(growth = (avg_price - lag(avg_price)) / lag(avg_price)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(sale_year %in% 2023:2025)
```
:::

`lag()` uses row order, so sort by year first.
